title: First aid for an eye injury
asks: something stuck in my eye what do I do
bleach splashed in eye how long to rinse
stick poked my eye and it is bleeding
metal fragment in eye do I pull it out
how to cover an injured eye
somthing in eye wont come out
can I put a patch on a hurt eye
answer: Chemical in the eye: IMMEDIATELY flood the eye with water. Keep irrigating with running water from a faucet, low-pressure hose, bottle or cup, gently from the inner corner (nearest the nose) to the outer corner (towards the ear).
Chemical in the eye: keep washing the eye out for at least 20 minutes or until you reach medical care, and keep washing during transport. After flushing, get the person evacuated immediately.

Any eye injury should be evaluated and treated by a medical professional as soon as possible. If a penetrating eye injury is seen or suspected, do not waste critical time on further treatment: shield the eye and get the person evacuated as soon as possible.

Suspect a penetrating eye injury if there is bleeding around, inside or from the eyeball, something sticking into or out of the eyeball, a swollen, cut, misshapen or protruding eyeball, or reduced vision with swelling of the eye area.
Unless it is a chemical injury, do not put anything on the eye itself, do not put pressure on the eye, do not touch or rub it, and do not remove anything from the eye surface.
Sit a conscious person up. Lay an unconscious person on their back with the head slightly raised. Gently clean any dirt or blood from the area around the eye.

Cover the injured eye with a rigid eye shield, not a pressure patch, or with anything that gives a hard cover over the eye: protective glasses or goggles, or the bottom of a disposable cup. Secure it with tape from the cheek to the forehead; if there is no tape, use gauze, cloth, a shoelace or string.
Object stuck in the eye: do not remove it. Build dry sterile dressings up around the object to support it, then cover the eye with a paper cup or cardboard cone.

Eyeball out of its socket: do not try to put it back. Lay the person face up. Cut a hole in several layers of dressing and moisten it with the cleanest water available; place it so the eyeball protrudes through the hole with minimal contact, build the dressing up higher than the eyeball, and cover with a paper cup or cardboard cone that does not touch the eye. Call for medical aid immediately.
Move the person on their back with the head raised and kept still, and bring their eyeglasses even if they are broken.
warnings: Do not press on an injured eye. The eyeball contains fluid; pressure over the eye will force the fluid out and cause permanent injury. A pressure dressing could result in permanent loss of vision.
Never place anything under the eye shield or directly on the eye.

Do not try to remove an object stuck to or sticking into the eyeball. Only something loose on the surface that comes away easily, such as an eyelash or a speck of dirt, may be removed by the injured person.
Do not force the eyelids open.
Burns of the eyelids or face: do not apply a dressing, do not touch, and seek medical assistance immediately. Do not try to force open eyes with thermal burns.

quotes.text: IMMEDIATELY flood the eye with water. • Keep irrigating the eye with running water from a faucet, low-pressure hose, bottle, cup, or intravenous setup (if available). • Hold the irrigating tip 1 to 1½ inches away from the casualty's eye or eyes, direct the irrigating solution gently from the inner eye (nearest the nose) to the outer eye (towards the ear) from the casualty's unaffected eye. • Start the transport and continue washing out the eye or eyes for at least 20 minutes or until the casualty's arrival at the MTF.

If the burn is an acid burn, you should flush the eye for at least 5 to 10 minutes. If the burn is an alkali burn, you should flush the eye for at least 20 minutes. After the eye has been flushed, evacuate the casualty immediately.
Eye trauma should always be evaluated and treated by a qualified medical professional as soon as possible.
If a penetrating eye injury is seen or suspected, the first responder must shield the injured eye. The casualties injured eye must be covered with a rigid eye shield, not a pressure patch.

If there is a protruding object in the eye, bandage in place — do not remove the object. Do not waste critical time by conducting further treatment. The casualty should be evacuated as soon as possible.
Survey the situation; if the injury is from chemical exposure, immediately wash the eye. Otherwise, DO NOT put anything on the eye ITSELF, especially if you think the eye is cut.
DO NOT put pressure on the eye or remove anything from the eye surface. This could cause additional harm, such as loss of eyesight or loss of the eye.
Avoid touching or rubbing the eye, as this can exacerbate the damage. Place a protective shield or cup over the eye, if available, to prevent accidental contact.

The following signs should make you suspect a penetrating eye injury: • Bleeding surrounding the eye, inside the eyeball, or coming from the eyeball. • Obvious penetration of shrapnel or debris into the eyeball or eye socket. • Protruding objects from the globe of the eyeball. • Swelling or lacerations of the globe of the eyeball. • Protrusion of the globe of the eyeball from the eye socket. • Reduced vision and swelling of the eye area. • Misshapen or distorted parts of the eye from normal.

Position and treat the casualty as follows: • The conscious casualty will be placed in a seated position. • The unconscious casualty will be placed in a supine position with their head slightly elevated. • Gently clean any dirt or blood from the affected area around the eye.

Use the rigid eye-shield provided in the first aid kit, or anything that provides a hard cover over the eye, such as— • Eye protective gear, ballistic glasses, or goggles. • The bottom of a disposable cup, for example one made of extruded polystyrene (foam), plastic, or paper. Note. This helps prevent any undue pressure or further damage to the eye. DO NOT put any pressure on the eye. • Secure the rigid eye-shield by applying tape from the cheek to the forehead. If tape is unavailable, use gauze, cloth dressing, shoelace, or string to secure in place.
ALWAYS use a rigid eye-shield to provide a barrier to prevent further damage. NEVER place anything under the rigid eye-shield or directly on the eye.

DO NOT attempt to remove a foreign object stuck to or sticking into the eyeball. A medical officer (physician) must remove such objects. 10-24. Apply dry sterile dressings to build around and support the object. This will help prevent further contamination and minimize movement of the object. Cover the injured eye with a paper cup or cardboard cone. 10-25. Seek further medical aid immediately.

Foreign bodies in the eye are treated by appropriate medical personnel or by the casualty if it can easily be removed (for example, a surface non-embedded material such as an eyelash or speck of dirt).

DO NOT attempt to reposition the eyeball or replace it in the eye socket. 10-36. Provide appropriate first aid for the injury as follows: • Position the casualty face up. • Cut a hole into several layers of dressing material and then moisten it. Use sterile or the cleanest water if available, preferably potable.

Gently place the dressing so the injured eyeball protrudes through the hole, with minimal contact. Surround and protect the eyeball, minimizing the movement of the dressing. The dressing should be built up higher than the eyeball. Note. If available, place a paper cup or cone-shaped piece of cardboard over the eye. This material should not touch the eye. Do not apply pressure to the injury site. Apply roller gauze to hold the cup in place.
Call for medical aid immediately and arrange for MEDEVAC as soon as possible.
Evacuate the casualty: • On their back, with the head elevated and immobilized. • With their corrective eyeglasses, even if they are broken.
DO NOT apply pressure when there is a possible laceration of the eyeball. The eyeball contains fluid. Pressure applied over the eye will force the fluid out, resulting in permanent injury.
Cover the affected eye with a rigid eye shield, NOT a pressure patch. A pressure dressing could result in permanent loss of vision.

Ask the casualty if they are wearing contact lenses, but DO NOT force the eyelids open. Record and communicate to medical personnel (first responders, emergency medical technicians, or combat medics) that contact lenses are being worn.
If a casualty receives burns of the eyelids or face— • DO NOT apply dressing. • DO NOT touch. • SEEK medical assistance immediately. WARNING DO NOT attempt to force open the eyes with thermal burns.

conflict: COVERING THE UNINJURED EYE (the card says nothing about it): ATP 4-02.11 (2026) paras 10-5 to 10-7 and 10-52 say shield the injured eye only, not both, and do not cover the uninjured eye to prevent eye movement; JTS Eye Trauma Initial Care 2021 says 'Shield ONLY injured eye'; JTS Ocular Injuries PFC 2017 says patching both eyes has not been shown to improve outcome. But ATP 4-02.11 para 10-21 says with impaled objects both eyes are usually bandaged (uninjured eye left uncovered on a battlefield) and para 10-31 says cover the unaffected eye when the eyeball is out of its socket; ATP 3-50.21 (2018) says 'Cover both eyes because the eyes are sympathetic'; WHO-ICRC Basic Emergency Care 2018 says place a loose patch over both eyes. SHIELD OR DRESSING: ATP 4-02.11 cautions never to place anything under the shield or directly on the eye, yet its paras 10-8 and 10-9 say cover a lacerated eyelid or eyeball with a (loose) sterile dressing without pressure; WHO BEC says a loose patch. The card uses the rigid shield only. FLUSH TIME for chemicals: ATP 4-02.11 para 10-41 says at least 5 to 20 minutes (acid at least 5 to 10, alkali at least 20) and para 10-46 says at least 20 minutes or until arrival; the card gives the 20-minute figure. JTS Eye Trauma gives volumes instead (minimum 2 liters, up to 10). HHS Ship's Medicine Chest 2003 (only 'copious saline irrigation' for chemical agents in the eye) and FEMA P-2064 (2020) add no eye first aid.

review.notes: Confirmed in context: ATP 4-02.11 ch. 10 (chemical: flood immediately, inner to outer corner, at least 20 minutes or until arrival, evacuate after flushing; acid 5-10 / alkali 20 min; penetrating-injury signs; nothing on the eye, no pressure, no rubbing, nothing removed; positions; rigid shield not pressure patch, improvised cup, taping; impaled object built around; extruded eyeball dressing; evacuate on the back, head raised, with glasses; do not force lids; eyelid/face burns). Chemical flushing comes first, which is the most urgent action. Both-eyes, shield-vs-dressing and flush-time disagreements are listed. No PDF junk. Minor: A5 'do not remove anything from the eye surface' and W3 (the injured person may remove an eyelash or speck) read as a contradiction at first glance; put W3's exception directly after A5.
